latest.summary: It is possible to switch to a better tariff and save money despite the forecast rise next year Average energy bill in Great Britain predicted to rise to £2,166 The energy price cap in Great Britain looks likely to go up by 26% in January . But your bills might not have to rise by the same amount. If you are paying a tariff that matches the price cap you could save by switching to something lower. And if you do it now, you could make a substantial saving. Providers are offering fixed tariffs that work out up to £407 below the estimated price cap, according to price comparison website uSwitch. It’s worth noting that it’s the price of the energy you use that is fixed, not your bill – so you will still be charged according to what you use. Continue reading...

World.title: Apec summit live: Xi welcomes Trump on China visit as Putin claims Europe in ‘humiliating decline’
World.summary: Summit in Chinese tech hub Shenzhen set to include highly anticipated meeting between Xi, Trump and Putin Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit What is Apec? Explained in 30 seconds Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up? That is the question the Guardian’s diplomatic correspondent Patrick Wintour seeks to address in his piece about the expected, Putin, Trump and Xi, meeting at Apec on Thursday. It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran, have reason to be nervous that their sponsors might abandon them in a complex geopolitical trade-off that Putin envisions, and Trump seems to endorse. Science.title: MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system
Science.summary: MIT researchers have discovered that the brain’s natural waste-removal system becomes significantly less effective during sleep as people age. The decline is linked to weaker deep-sleep brain waves and changes in blood flow, potentially offering new clues about why aging increases the risk of Alzheimer's disease and dementia. Surprisingly, some older adults retain the same powerful cleansing waves seen in younger people.

Science.title: A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s
Science.summary: Scientists have uncovered a powerful natural defense against Alzheimer’s disease that could open the door to new treatments. By boosting a protein called SORLA, researchers significantly reduced toxic tau tangles, protected connections between brain cells, and prevented some of the brain shrinkage associated with neurodegeneration in mice. Removing the protein made the damage worse, highlighting its critical protective role.

Culture.title: ‘Everything he said sounded like a song title!’ The rackety, romantic life of Bobby Charles, alligator-befriending bard of the bayou
Culture.summary: He was nearly an early rock’n’roll star but took a different path, from Fats Domino to the Band and pro-environment songwriting. As a career-spanning box set is released, those who knew him remember an American original ‘I was listening to Bob Dylan’s Theme Time radio show,” says Korey Richey, multi-instrumentalist with LCD Soundsystem, “and he said, ‘Bobby Charles is best known as a songwriter, but he has one of the most melodious voices ever transmuted into a piece of vinyl.’ I thought about it, and I agree: Bobby Charles was something else.” Something else, indeed. Charles (1938–2010) was unable to play an instrument yet wrote songs sung by everyone from Fats Domino to Etta James to Kris Kristofferson. Signed to Chess Records in 1955 aged 17, he was on the verge of becoming a star at the dawn of rock’n’roll, but a preference for living reclusively – with a pet alligator – ensured he vanished from sight, and his music has long been unavailable. “He was a very strange guy, a loner,” says one of his Louisiana contemporaries, 88-year-old Johnnie Allan. “He knew what he had and wouldn’t compromise.” Now a box set, The Bobby Charles Story, containing almost every recording Charles released, aims to establish the Cajun magus as one of the greats. Culture.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
Culture.summary: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it. For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. Jason is muscular, handsome, ex-military, steady and unflappable, sincere but spare with words. Lucia has been boosting cars since the age of 14, has a wicked sense of humour and takes zero bullshit. (Lucia is the scarier one; I found myself turning much more quickly to violence when playing as her.) At the start, Lucia is incarcerated and Jason is making a go of things in the sunbeaten Keys, working for a dodgy guy down on the marina and renting a run-down house on stilts with a jetty round the back and a pet snake. When Lucia gets out of prison, the two of them try to make some kind of life for themselves – but before long they get caught up with the wrong people and have to flee the cosy life they’ve just started building.
